en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes, Section 7:
The Training Rule on "More Than That.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks approached monks whose robes had been stolen and said to them:
“Friends, it has been permitted by the Blessed One:
‘One whose robe has been stolen or one whose robe has been lost may request a robe from an unrelated householder or housewife.’”
“Friends, please request a robe.”—
“Enough, friend; we have already received a robe.”—
“We are requesting one for you, venerable sirs.”
“Inform them, friends.
Then the group-of-six monks, having approached the householders, said this to them:
“Friends, monks have arrived whose robes have been stolen.”
"Give them robes! they requested a great quantity of robes.
Now at that time, a certain man sitting in the assembly hall said this to another man:
“The noble monks have arrived with their robes torn;
I have given them a robe.
He too said, “I have given one as well.”
Another also said, "I have given as well.
They complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these Sakyan-son ascetics, lacking moderation, request so much robe-cloth?"
“The ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, will either engage in the trade of liquor or open a tavern.
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
“How can the group-of-six monks, failing to know moderation, request so much robe-cloth?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you, failing to know moderation, requested so much robe-cloth?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:

“… How can you, foolish men, not knowing moderation, request so many robes? This will lead to the decline of the true Dhamma. … [as before] … “How can you, foolish men, not knowing moderation, request so many robes?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … [as before] … And thus,
monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If an unrelated householder or housewife should invite one to accept many robes, one may accept at most an inner and an outer robe.’”
That monk may accept the robe from him. If he should accept it beyond that limit, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
"To him" means to a monk whose robes have been stolen.
A "stranger" (aññātaka) is one who is not related by descent from the mother’s side or the father’s side, up to the seventh generation on the paternal line.
A "householder" (gahapati) is...
Whoever dwells in a house is a householder. Whoever,
being female, dwells in a house is called a housewife.
"With many robes" means with numerous robes.
"One should invite [the donor] to bring them" means...
"Take as much as you wish.
A monk may accept robe-cloth from that person up to the limit of one inner and one outer robe.
If three robes have been lost, two may be accepted; if two have been lost, one may be accepted; if only one has been lost, nothing may be accepted.
“If she should accept more than that” means:
if she requests more than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act;
by the acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
It is to be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, it is to be relinquished:
…pe…
“Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which was requested from more than one unrelated householder after he had approached them, is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. …pe… “He should give it back,” …pe…
"May he give... ... [and so on] ... "I give it to the Venerable One.
If, regarding one who is not related, he perceives that person as not being related, and he requests a robe exceeding [the permitted amount], it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If he requests more than that amount of robe-cloth from one who is unrelated to him, while being in doubt [about his relationship], it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If he requests more than that amount of robe-cloth from one who is unrelated to him, perceiving him as related, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession. If he requests more than that amount of robe-cloth from one who is related to him, perceiving him as unrelated, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he is doubtful regarding a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he is a relative and perceives him as such, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If he goes away intending, "I will take the remainder," and they give it to him,
saying, "Let the remainder be yours alone," they do not give it because of a prior refusal.
They do not give because of loss,
nor to relatives,
nor to those who have already been invited.
With one's own wealth;
for one who is insane;
for the first offender.
The seventh training rule, which follows that, is concluded.
